# Kāyagatāsati Sutta (MN 119 (PTS MN iii 88))

**ID:** MN 119 (PTS MN iii 88)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Kāyagatāsati Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** Mindfulness of the Body  
**PTS:** MN iii 88  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāyagatāsati Sutta* (MN 119, PTS MN iii 88) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* dedicated entirely to the cultivation and benefits of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā sati*) [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2014]. In sutta usage, *kāyagatā sati* broadly encompasses all meditation exercises based on the physical body, unlike the later commentarial tradition which often restricts the term specifically to contemplation of the thirty-two bodily parts [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2012]. The text presents an array of bodily contemplations—beginning with the first four steps of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*), bodily postures, clear comprehension, anatomical parts, elements, and charnel-ground meditations—and notably includes the attainment of the four absorptions (*jhāna*), highlighting the physical experience and bodily pervasive bliss accompanying these meditative absorptions [Anālayo 2003; Anālayo 2019; Polak 2011]. A recurring refrain emphasizes how the mind settles, becomes concentrated, and sheds worldly memories and intentions through each practice, leading to numerous beneficial qualities and mental detachment [Shulman 2014; Anālayo 2014].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MA 81 念身
- Resembling parallels: DN 22 (PTS DN ii 290) Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; EA 12.1 ?; MA 98 念處; MN 10 (PTS MN i 55) Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; SHT Sutta 11; MA 31 分別聖諦; T 32 四諦

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Discusses sutta usage of kāyagatā sati versus commentarial restriction to thirty-two bodily parts.
- [Bodhi 2012] Bhikkhu Bodhi, Numerical Discourses of the Buddha (2012) — Mentions kāyagatāsati in the broad sense of MN 119 covering all body meditations.
- [Anālayo 2003] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Satipatthana: The Direct Path to Realization (2003) — Examines inclusion of the four absorptions under body contemplation.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipatthana (2014) — Analyzes the relationship with the Madhyama-āgama parallel, gaining concentration, and similes of benefits.
- [Anālayo 2019] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfulness of Breathing (2019) — Examines reduction of mindfulness of breathing to the first tetrad and absorption descriptions.
- [Kuan 2008] Tse-fu Kuan, Mindfulness in Early Buddhism (2008) — Identifies the Chinese parallel Nianshen Jing (MĀ 98) and compares practices.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhana (2011) — Details presence of the basic first tetrad of ānāpānasati in MN 119.
- [Shulman 2014] Eviatar Shulman, Rethinking the Buddha (2014) — Cites the refrain at MN iii 88–94 on mental concentration and internalizing skillful qualities.
